questions.stem: In the sentence 'Although it was raining, we still went outside', the words 'Although it was raining' form:

options.text: a subordinate part, which cannot stand alone
a complete sentence on their own

questions.explanation: 'Although it was raining' cannot stand alone and leans on the main clause 'we still went outside', so it is a subordinate clause.

questions.stem: What type of sentence is 'Please shut the gate behind you.'?
questions.explanation: It tells someone to do something, so it is a command (an imperative), even though it opens politely with 'Please'.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: 'You ___ wear a helmet when you cycle; here it is the law.'
questions.explanation: The law makes it an obligation, and 'must' expresses that duty most strongly.

questions.stem: Which phrase is correctly hyphenated?
questions.explanation: 'Well-known' is a compound adjective before the noun 'actor', so its two parts are joined with a single hyphen.

questions.stem: In 'The children cheered because their team had won', what kind of clause is 'because their team had won'?
questions.explanation: It explains WHY the children cheered, doing the job of an adverb, so it is an adverbial clause of reason.

questions.stem: What type of sentence is 'What a wonderful surprise this is!'?
questions.explanation: It expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark, so it is an exclamation.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: 'The sky is grey, so it ___ rain before evening.'
questions.explanation: A grey sky makes rain possible but not certain, and 'might' expresses that possibility.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?

options.text: There are thirty two children in my brother in law's class.
There are thirty-two children in my brother in-law's class.
There are thirty-two children in my brother-in-law's class.
There are thirty two-children in my brotherinlaw's class.
There are thirty-two-children in my brother-in-laws class.

questions.explanation: 'Thirty-two' (a compound number) and 'brother-in-law' (a compound noun) each join all their parts with hyphens.

questions.stem: In 'The vase on the high shelf wobbled', the words 'on the high shelf' are:
questions.explanation: 'On the high shelf' has no verb of its own, so it is a phrase, not a clause -- here a prepositional phrase describing the vase.

questions.stem: 'Water boils at one hundred degrees.' This sentence is:
questions.explanation: It simply tells us a fact, so it is a statement (a declarative sentence).

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If I ___ in charge, I would change the rules.'
questions.explanation: In this kind of imagined 'if' sentence, standard English uses the subjunctive 'were', not 'was'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pair of brackets correctly?

options.text: My grandmother (who is eighty still swims every day.
My grandmother who is eighty) still swims every day.
My grandmother (who is eighty) still swims every day.
My grandmother (who is eighty) still swims every day).
My (grandmother who is eighty) still swims every day.

questions.explanation: Brackets come as a matching pair, opening before the extra information and closing straight after it: '(who is eighty)'.

questions.stem: In 'What the letter contained shocked her', the words 'What the letter contained' work as:

options.text: the subject of the whole sentence
the main verb of the sentence

questions.explanation: 'What the letter contained' names the thing that shocked her; it does the work of a noun and is the subject, so it is a noun clause.

questions.stem: 'Would you mind closing the window.' Although it opens like a question, this sentence really works as:

options.text: a genuine question expecting yes or no

questions.explanation: It is a courteous way of telling someone to close the window, so it functions as a polite command rather than a real question.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'The head insisted that every pupil ___ on time for the exam.'
questions.explanation: After 'insisted that', formal English uses the subjunctive base form: 'that every pupil be on time'.

questions.stem: A pair of dashes can mark off extra information. Which sentence uses them correctly?

options.text: The champion -- a boy from our school, lifted the trophy high.
The champion, a boy from our school -- lifted the trophy high.
The champion -- a boy from our school lifted the trophy high.
The champion a boy -- from our school -- lifted the trophy high.
The champion -- a boy from our school -- lifted the trophy high.

questions.explanation: Like a pair of brackets, dashes that mark off extra information must come as a matching pair, one before and one after.

questions.stem: Which of these groups of words is a main clause that could stand alone as a sentence?
questions.explanation: 'The storm finally passed' makes complete sense on its own; the others each begin with a joining word and need a main clause to finish them.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences is a question?
questions.explanation: Only 'Have you finished your homework?' asks something and ends with a question mark.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: 'When she was younger, she ___ run a mile without stopping.'
questions.explanation: 'Could' expresses an ability she had in the past.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the hyphen give the intended meaning, 'covered again'?

options.text: We recovered the worn armchair in bright new fabric.
We re covered the worn armchair in bright new fabric.
We recover-ed the worn armchair in new fabric.
We re-covered the worn armchair in bright new fabric.
We-recovered the worn armchair in new fabric.

questions.explanation: 'Re-covered', with a hyphen, means covered again; 'recovered' without one means got better or got back -- so the hyphen changes the meaning.

questions.stem: In 'The parcel that arrived today is for you', the words 'that arrived today' are:
questions.explanation: 'That arrived today' gives more information about the noun 'parcel', so it is a relative clause.

questions.stem: 'Never had she seen such a sight.' Despite its unusual, inverted word order, this sentence is:
questions.explanation: It still simply reports something that happened; the words are turned around for effect, but it remains a statement.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: 'You ___ have warned me it was a trap -- now look what has happened!'
questions.explanation: 'Should have' shows that warning was the right thing to do but it did not happen; it expresses regret or reproach.

questions.stem: Which word is written with hyphens in the correct places?
questions.explanation: 'Mother-in-law' joins its three parts with a hyphen between each.

questions.stem: Which of these is a phrase rather than a clause?
questions.explanation: 'Under the old oak tree' has no subject and verb, so it is a phrase; each of the others contains a subject and a verb, making it a clause.
